upsilon: The 20th letter (U, u) of the Greek alphabet, a vowel having originally the sound of oo as in room, becoming before the 4th century b. c. that French u or Ger. ü. Its equivalent in English is u or y.
upupa: A genus of birds which includes the common hoopoe.
uppish: Proud; arrogant; assuming; putting on airs of superiority. [Colloq.] T. Brown. -- Up"pish*ly, adv. [Colloq.] -- Up"pish*ness, n. [Colloq.]
upstay: To sustain; to support. (old) "His massy spear upstayed." Milton.
upover: Designating a method of shaft excavation by drifting to a point below, and then raising instead of sinking.
uptrain: 1. A train going in the direction of the metropolis or the main terminus. [Eng.] 2. A train going in the direction conventionally called up. [U.S.]
uplean: To lean or incline upon anything. (old) Spenser.
upsodown: Upside down. [Obs. or Colloq.] Wyclif. In man's sin is every manner order or ordinance turned upsodown. Chaucer.
uprising: 1. Act of rising; also, a steep place; an ascent. "The steep uprising of the hill." Shak. 2. An insurrection; a popular revolt. J. P. Peters.
uplandish: Of or pertaining to uplands; dwelling on high lands. (old) Chapman. 2. Rude; rustic; unpolished; uncivilized. (old) His presence made the rudest peasant melt, That in the wild, uplandish country dwelt. Marlowe.
upflow: To flow or stream up. Southey.
uppertendom: The highest class in society; the upper ten. See Upper ten, under Upper. [Colloq.]
upstand: To stand up; to be erected; to rise. Spenser. Milton. At once upstood the monarch, and upstood The wise Ulysses. Cowper.
upspurner: A spurner or contemner; a despiser; a scoffer. (old) Joye.
uphasp: To hasp or faster up; to close; as, sleep uphasps the eyes. Stanyhurst.
upcast: Cast up; thrown upward; as, with upcast eyes. Addison. | 1. (Bowling) A cast; a throw. Shak. 2. (Mining.) The ventilating shaft of a mine out of which the air passes after having circulated through the mine; -- distinguished from the downcast.
upridged: Raised up in a ridge or ridges; as, a billow upridged. Cowper.
upswarm: To rise, or cause to rise, in a swarm or swarms. Shak. Cowper.
upon: On; -- used in all the senses of that word, with which it is interchangeable. "Upon an hill of flowers." Chaucer. Our host upon his stirrups stood anon. Chaucer. Thou shalt take of the blood that is upon the altar. Ex. xxix. 21. The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. Judg. xvi. 9. As I did stand my watch upon the hill. Shak.
upsend: To send, cast, or throw up. As when some island situate afar . . . Upsends a smoke to heaven. Cowper.
upwreath: To rise with a curling motion; to curl upward, as smoke. Longfellow.
upholder: 1. A broker or auctioneer; a tradesman. (old) 2. An undertaker, or provider for funerals. (old) The upholder, rueful harbinger of death. Gay. 3. An upholsterer. (old) 4. One who, or that which, upholds; a supporter; a defender; a sustainer.
upbuoyance: The act of buoying up; uplifting. Coleridge.
upsetting: Conceited; assuming; as, an upsetting fellow. [Scot.] Jamieson.
uphand: Lifted by the hand, or by both hands; as, the uphand sledge. Moxon.
uproar: Great tumult; violent disturbance and noise; noisy confusion; bustle and clamor. But the Jews which believed not, . . . set all the city on an uproar. Acts xvii. 5. | To throw into uproar or confusion. (old) "Uproar the universal peace." Shak.
upclimb: To climb up; to ascend. Upclomb the shadowy pine above the woven copse. Tennyson.
upcountry: In an upcountry direction; as, to live upcountry. [Colloq.] | Living or situated remote from the seacoast; as, an upcountry residence. [Colloq.] -- n. The interior of the country. [Colloq.]
upbreathe: To breathe up or out; to exhale. (old) Marston.
uprist: imp. of Uprise. Uprose. Chaucer. Nor dim nor red, like God's own head The glorious sun uprist. Coleridge.
upturn: To turn up; to direct upward; to throw up; as, to upturn the ground in plowing. "A sea of upturned faces." D. Webster. So scented the grim feature, and upturned His nostril wide into the murky air. Milton.
uptake: To take into the hand; to take up; to help. (old) Wyclif. Spenser. | 1. The pipe leading upward from the smoke box of a steam boiler to the chimney, or smokestack; a flue leading upward. 2. Understanding; apprehension. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.
upend: To end up; to set on end, as a cask.
upbar: 1. To fasten with a bar. 2. To remove the bar or bards of, as a gate; to under. (old) Spenser.
uptailsall: 1. An old game at cards. (old) 2. Revelers; roysterers. (old) Decker. 3. Revelry; confusion; frolic. (old) Herrick.
upgrowth: The process or result of growing up; progress; development. The new and mighty upgrowth of poetry in Italy. J. R. Green.
upsoar: To soar or mount up. Pope.
upside: The upper side; the part that is uppermost. To be upsides with, to be even with. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Sir W. Scott. T. Hughes. -- Upside down. Etym: [Perhaps a corruption of OE. up so down, literally, up as down.] With the upper part undermost; hence, in confusion; in complete disorder; topsy-turvy. Shak. These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also.
upheave: To heave or lift up from beneath; to raise. Milton.
upas: 1. (Bot.) A tree (Antiaris toxicaria) of the Breadfruit family, common in the forests of Java and the neighboring islands. Its secretions are poisonous, and it has been fabulously reported that the atmosphere about it is deleterious. Called also bohun upas. 2. A virulent poison used in Java and the adjacent islands for poisoning arrows.
upokororo: An edible fresh-water New Zealand fish (Prototroctes oxyrhynchus) of the family Haplochitonidæ. In general appearance and habits, it resembles the northern lake whitefishes and trout. Called also grayling.
upsettingthermometer: A thermometer by merely inverting which the temperature may be registered. The column of mercury is broken and, as it remains until the instrument is reset, the reading may be made at leisure.
upkeep: The act of keeping up, or maintaining; maintenance. "Horse artillery . . . expensive in the upkeep." Scribner's Mag. Small outlays for repairs or upkeep of buildings. A. R. Colquhoun.
uproot: To root up; to tear up by the roots, or as if by the roots; to remove utterly; to eradicate; to extirpate. Trees uprooted left their place. Dryden. At his command the uprooted hills retired. Milton.
upland: 1. High land; ground elevated above the meadows and intervals which lie on the banks of rivers, near the sea, or between hills; land which is generally dry; -- opposed to lowland, meadow, marsh,… | 1. Of or pertaining to uplands; being on upland; high in situation; as, upland inhabitants; upland pasturage. Sometimes, with secure delight The upland hamlets will invite. Milton. 2.
upright: 1. In an erect position or posture; perpendicular; vertical, or nearly vertical; pointing upward; as, an upright tree. With chattering teeth, and bristling hair upright. Dryden. | Something standing upright, as a piece of timber in a building. See Illust. of Frame.
upspear: To grow or shoot up like a spear; as, upspearing grass. Cowper.
upblow: To blow up; as, the wind upblows from the sea. (old) Spenser.
upburst: The act of bursting upwards; a breaking through to the surface; an upbreak or uprush; as, an upburst of molten matter.
upgather: To gather up; to contract; to draw together. (old) Himself he close upgathered more and more. Spenser.
uphold: 1. To hold up; to lift on high; to elevate. The mournful train with groans, and hands upheld. Besought his pity. Dryden. 2. To keep erect; to support; to sustain; to keep from falling; to maintain. Honor shall uphold the humble in spirit. Prov. xxix 3. Faulconbridge, In spite of spite, alone upholds the day. Shak. 3. To aid by approval or encouragement; to countenance;
upstare: To stare or stand upward; hence, to be uplifted or conspicuous. "Rearing fiercely their upstaring crests." Spenser.
uprouse: To rouse up; to rouse from sleep; to awake; to arouse. Shak.
upshot: Final issue; conclusion; the sum and substance; the end; the result; the consummation. I can not pursue with any safety this sport to the upshot. Shak. We account it frailty that threescore years and ten make the upshot of man's pleasurable existence. De Quincey.
upstream: Toward the higher part of a stream; against the current.
upbear: To bear up; to raise aloft; to support in an elevated situation; to sustain. Spenser. One short sigh of breath, upbore Even to the seat of God. Milton. A monstrous wave upbore The chief, and dashed him on the craggy shore. Pope.
upspring: 1. An upstart. (old) "The swaggering upspring." Shak. 2. A spring or leap into the air. Chapman.
uppricked: Upraised; erect; -- said of the ears of an animal. Mason.
upstreet: Toward the higher part of a street; as, to walk upstreet. G. W. Gable.
upstart: To start or spring up suddenly. Spenser. Tennyson. | 1. One who has risen suddenly, as from low life to wealth, power, or honor; a parvenu. Bacon. 2. (Bot.) The meadow saffron. Dr. Prior.
uplander: 1. One dwelling in the upland; hence, a countryman; a rustic. (old) 2. (Zoöl.) The upland sandpiper. [Local, U. S.]
uptodate: Extending to the present time; having style, manners, knowledge, or other qualities that are abreast of the times. "A general up-to-date style of presentment." Nature. I must prefer to translate the poet in a manner more congenial if less up-to-date. Andrew Lang.
upsun: The time during which the sun is up, or above the horizon; the time between sunrise and sunset.
upcaught: Seized or caught up. " She bears upcaught a mariner away." Cowper.
upseek: To seek or strain upward. "Upseeking eyes suffused with . . . tears." Southey.
uplift: To lift or raise aloft; to raise; to elevate; as, to uplift the arm; to uplift a rock. Cowper. Satan, talking to his nearest mate, With head uplift above the wave, and eyes That sparkling blazed. | A raising or upheaval of strata so as to disturb their regularity and uniformity, and to occasion folds, dislocations, and the like.
uprush: Act of rushing upward; an upbreak or upburst; as, an uprush of lava. R. A. Proctor.
uppermost: Highest in place, position, rank, power, or the like; upmost; supreme. Whatever faction happens to be uppermost. Swift.
updive: To spring upward; to rise. Davies (Microcosmos).
upholsterer: One who provides hangings, coverings, cushions, curtains, and the like; one who upholsters. Upholsterer bee. (Zoöl.) See Poppy bee, under Poppy.
upper: Being further up, literally or figuratively; higher in place, position, rank, dignity, or the like; superior; as, the upper lip; the upper side of a thing; the upper house of a legislature. | The upper leather for a shoe; a vamp.
upholstery: The articles or goods supplied by upholsterers; the business or work of an upholsterer.
upher: A fir pole of from four to seven inches diameter, and twenty to forty feet long, sometimes roughly hewn, used for scaffoldings, and sometimes for slight and common roofs, for which use it is split. [Spelt also ufer.] [Eng.] Gwilt.
uproarious: Making, or accompanied by, uproar, or noise and tumult; as, uproarious merriment. -- Up*roar"i*ous*ly, adv. -- Up*roar"i*ous*ness, n.
up: 1. Aloft; on high; in a direction contrary to that of gravity; toward or in a higher place or position; above; -- the opposite of Ant: down. But up or down, By center or eccentric, hard to tell. | 1. From a lower to a higher place on, upon, or along; at a higher situation upon; at the top of. In going up a hill, the knees will be most weary; in going down, the thihgs. Bacon. 2.
upstroke: An upward stroke, especially the stroke, or line, made by a writing instrument when moving upward, or from the body of the writer, or a line corresponding to the part of a letter thus made. Some upstroke of an Alpha and Omega. Mrs. Browning.
uprise: 1. To rise; to get up; to appear from below the horizon. "Uprose the sun." Cowley. Uprose the virgin with the morning light. Pope. 2. To have an upward direction or inclination. | The act of rising; appearance above the horizon; rising. Did ever raven sing so like a lark, That gives sweet tidings of the sun's uprise Shak.
upbreak: To break upwards; to force away or passage to the surface. | A breaking upward or bursting forth; an upburst. Mrs. Browning.
upline: A line or track leading from the provinces toward the metropolis or a principal terminus; the track upon which up-trains run. See Up-train. [Eng.]
upwards: 1. In a direction from lower to higher; toward a higher place; in a course toward the source or origin; -- opposed to downward; as, to tend or roll upward. I. Watts. Looking inward, we are stricken dumb; looking upward, we speak and prevail. Hooker. 2. In the upper parts; above. Dagon his name, sea monster, upward man, And down ward fish. Milton. 3. Yet more;
uprighteously: In an upright or just manner. (old) Shak.
upstairs: Up the stairs; in or toward an upper story. | Being above stairs; as, an upstairs room.
uphilt: To thrust in up to the hilt; as, to uphilt one's sword into an enemy. Stanyhurst.
upstir: Insurrection; commotion; disturbance. (old) Sir J. Cheke.
upthrow: To throw up. Drayton. | See Throw, n., 9.
upbraid: 1. To charge with something wrong or disgraceful; to reproach; to cast something in the teeth of; -- followed by with or for, and formerly of, before the thing imputed. | The act of reproaching; contumely. (old) " Foul upbraid." Spenser.
upholster: To furnish (rooms, carriages, bedsteads, chairs, etc.) with hangings, coverings, cushions, etc.; to adorn with furnishings in cloth, velvet, silk, etc.; as, to upholster a couch; | 1. A broker. (old) Caxton. 2. An upholsterer. (old) Strype.
upheaped: Piled up; accumulated. God, which shall repay all with upheaped measure. Udall.
upshoot: To shoot upward. "Trees upshooting high." Spenser.
upset: 1. To set up; to put upright. (old) "With sail on mast upset." R. of Brunne. 2. (a) To thicken and shorten, as a heated piece of iron, by hammering on the end. (b) To shorten (a tire) in the process… | Set up; fixed; determined; -- used chiefly or only in the phrase upset price; that is, the price fixed upon as the minimum for property offered in a public sale, or, in an auction, the price at which…
upcoil: To coil up; to make into a coil, or to be made into a coil.
upgush: A gushing upward. Hawthorne. | To gush upward.
upheaval: The act of upheaving, or the state of being upheaved; esp., an elevation of a portion of the earth's crust. Lubbock.
uprightness: the quality or state of being upright.
upsway: To sway or swing aloft; as, to upsway a club. Sir W. Scott.
upsitting: A sitting up of a woman after her confinement, to receive and entertain her friends. (old) To invite your lady's upsitting. Beau. & Fl.
upwhirl: To rise upward in a whirl; to raise upward with a whirling motion.
upward: 1. In a direction from lower to higher; toward a higher place; in a course toward the source or origin; -- opposed to downward; as, to tend or roll upward. I. Watts. | Directed toward a higher place; as, with upward eye; with upward course.
upbreed: To rear, or bring up; to nurse. "Upbred in a foreign country." Holinshed.
upthunder: To send up a noise like thunder. Coleridge.
uptill: To; against. [Obs. & R.] She, poor bird, as all forlorn, Leaned her breast uptill a thorn. Shak.
uphill: Upwards on, or as on, a hillside; as, to walk uphill. | 1. Ascending; going up; as, an uphill road. 2. Attended with labor; difficult; as, uphill work.
uptown: To or in the upper part of a town; as, to go uptown. [Colloq. U. S.] | Situated in, or belonging to, the upper part of a town or city; as, a uptown street, shop, etc.; uptown society. [Colloq. U. S.]
uppile: To pile, or heap, up. Southey.
uprun: To run up; to ascend. The young sun That in the Ram is four degrees uprun. Chaucer. [A son] of matchless might, who, like a thriving plant, Upran to manhood. Cowper.
